name: Old Cham
confidence_why: Old Cham survives only in inscriptions, which say nothing about stress (Aymonier 1891; Griffiths, Lepoutre, Southworth and Thanh Phan 2012), and the one statement in reach, Thurgood's (1996, 1999) reconstruction of word-final stress for Proto-Chamic, concerns the reconstructed ancestor and the modern dialects rather than the inscriptional language, as Griffiths et al. (2012) themselves point out, so any placement for Old Cham would be inferred rather than described.

catalog_quote: [Thurgood 1996, preprint p. 4] Under the influence of the Mon-Khmer (MK) languages along the coast of southeastern Vietnam, pre-Chamic quickly developed into a PC with final stress, resulting in disyllabic roots consisting of an unstressed initial syllable followed by a stressed main syllable. The stress pattern is reflected in the vowel inventories reconstructable for the PC disyllables ... The fact that most of these reconstruct to the PC stage is of some significance, for it places the borrowings ... roughly 2,000 years ago, a date given support by the oldest inscription in a Cham language, found at the site of modern-day Tra-kiêu ... which Coedès (1968:48) dates as from the middle of the fourth century AD. [preprint p. 6] ... the introduction of final stress into PC under MK influence, producing iambic words consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable. [Thurgood 1999 p. 106] ... unstressed atonic presyllable followed by an enriched, stressed tonic syllable. Under the influence of contact with neighboring MK languages, pre-Chamic developed word-final stress, leading to the proliferation of contrasts in the stressed final syllable and eventually to the reduction of contrasts in the unstressed syllable. [p. 61] ... final stress under MK influence. Once the canonical preference was set for stress on the final syllable, the preconditions had been set up for the restructuring of the Chamic lexicon.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Reconstruction for pre-Chamic/Proto-Chamic, the ancestor of Old Cham: stress falls on the final (main) syllable of the disyllabic/sesquisyllabic word; the initial presyllable is unstressed and reduced (iambic, 'unstressed presyllable + stressed main syllable'). Old Cham, as the earliest attested Chamic stage (4th c. CE), would inherit this final-syllable stress, but no source states it for the inscriptional language directly.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in the snippets; Thurgood 1999 p. 141 notes some PC content words are monosyllabic (all with long vowels), which is trivially final-stressed. Thurgood 1999 pp. 150-151 rejects reconstructing PAn stress as the source of PC vowel length.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (canonical morpheme/lexical word shape), reconstructed historically from modern Chamic reflexes and Mon-Khmer contact; not from Old Cham inscriptional data, which is orthographic only. Snippets are Google Books scanned reached through the r.jina.ai reader proxy; end-of-line hyphenation ('sylla- ble') joined here, wording otherwise as shown.
new_statements.identity_note: Old Cham (oldc1255, ISO ocm) is the extinct epigraphic language of the Champa inscriptions (Dong Yen Chau, mid-4th c. CE, to c. 15th c.), attested only in writing. The quoted statement is Thurgood's (1999) reconstruction for pre-Chamic / Proto-Chamic (no glottocode; Chamic family = cham1330), the ancestor of Old Cham and of all modern Chamic languages, not a description of Old Cham itself; a stress value for oldc1255 would be an inference by inheritance. Do not confuse with modern Eastern Cham (cjm) / Western Cham (cja), the 'Written Cham' of Aymonier & Cabaton 1906 and Moussay 2006, for which direct descriptions exist.
